issues.legal_issue: Land earmarked for a proposed road remains subject to the owners’ established title when no road is formed and the land is neither acquired nor compensated.
material_facts: The owners had converted the land for non-agricultural use and formed a layout, with the disputed strip earmarked for a road.
No road was formed on the disputed strip, and the evidence showed that the strip had not been acquired and no compensation had been paid for it.
Municipal records, tax assessment extracts, a revision order setting aside cancellation of the khata, and oral evidence supported the owners’ title.
issues.conclusion: The owners established their title to the disputed strip and were entitled to a declaration of ownership; the High Court erred in denying that relief merely because the strip had been earmarked for a road.
issues.legal_principle: The evidence established that the land remained in the owners’ name and had not been acquired. Earmarking it for a road did not, on these facts, defeat their established title. No earlier case was cited for this issue.

rule.if: title_declaration_suit and land_earmarked_for_proposed_road and no_road_formed and no_acquisition_or_compensation and ownership_records_support_claim

predicates.title_declaration_suit: The owners brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of title to the disputed land.
predicates.land_earmarked_for_proposed_road: The owners set aside the disputed land for a proposed road.
predicates.no_road_formed: No road was formed on the disputed land.
predicates.no_acquisition_or_compensation: The competent authority did not acquire the disputed land or pay compensation for it.
predicates.ownership_records_support_claim: Property and tax records, together with other evidence, supported the owners’ claim of title.

issues.definition: When a title declaration suit concerns land earmarked for a proposed road, the road is not formed, the land is not acquired or compensated, and ownership records support the claim, the rule means that title is declared in the owners’ favour.

issues.legal_issue: A property owner is entitled to possession of an encroached portion when the encroachment is established by survey and inspection evidence.
material_facts: The owners alleged that the adjoining owners had encroached on part of the land earmarked for the road.
A land-records sketch, a court commissioner’s inspection and report, and other evidence supported the finding that the adjoining owners had encroached on a portion of the disputed land.
The first appellate court ordered delivery of possession of the portion proved to have been encroached.
issues.conclusion: The finding of encroachment was not perverse and should not have been disturbed; the order for delivery of possession was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the survey sketch, the court commissioner’s report and other evidence to uphold the factual finding of encroachment and the resulting possession order. No earlier case or specific provision was cited for this issue.

predicates.property_possession_claim: An owner sought possession of a portion of land allegedly occupied by another person.
predicates.survey_or_inspection_evidence_supports_e: A survey or inspection record supported the allegation that part of the owner’s land had been occupied.
predicates.encroachment_established: The evidence established that the adjoining occupier had encroached on the land.

issues.definition: When a property possession claim is supported by survey or inspection evidence establishing an encroachment, the rule means that possession of the encroached land is ordered for the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot disturb concurrent factual findings in a second appeal when those findings are supported by evidence and are not shown to be perverse.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concurrently found that the owners held title to the disputed land and that the adjoining owners had encroached on part of it.
Those findings were based on oral and documentary evidence, including ownership records, a survey sketch and a court commissioner’s report.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and altered the decree without identifying perversity in the concurrent findings or a substantial question of law warranting that interference.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no substantial ground to reappreciate the evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings; its judgment was set aside and the lower courts’ decree restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, concurrent findings of fact cannot be upset in a second appeal unless they are shown to be perverse. The court found no substantial question of law or other ground justifying reappreciation of the evidence. No earlier case was cited.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and findings_not_shown_perverse

predicates.second_appeal: The matter before the High Court was a second appeal from the lower courts’ decisions.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court made the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent findings rested on oral or documentary evidence in the record.
predicates.findings_not_shown_perverse: The findings were not shown to be perverse.

issues.definition: When a second appeal involves concurrent factual findings supported by evidence and not shown to be perverse, the rule means that High Court interference is unwarranted.
